title: The Classic 5-Stage Pipeline
summary: IF/ID/EX/MEM/WB — the textbook RISC pipeline, the registers that carry an instruction between stages, and why this exact five-way split.

slides.markdown:
The **classic 5-stage pipeline** (fetch, decode, execute, memory, write-back) is the reference design nearly every architecture course and interview question about pipelining is built on — it's the simplest pipeline that's still realistic.

Between every pair of stages sits a **pipeline register** — a small latch that freezes an instruction's data and control signals for exactly one cycle, so the next stage always reads a stable snapshot instead of a value still changing mid-cycle.

slides.subTitle: IF, ID, EX, MEM, WB
slides.markdown:
- **IF (Instruction Fetch)** — read the instruction word from memory at the address in the PC.
- **ID (Instruction Decode)** — split out the opcode and operands, read the register file.
- **EX (Execute)** — the ALU computes a result, or an address for a load/store, or resolves a branch condition.
- **MEM (Memory access)** — only load/store instructions actually touch memory here; others pass through untouched.
- **WB (Write-back)** — the result lands back in the register file.

Every instruction marches through all five stages in order, even ones that don't need a particular stage's work.

slides.subTitle: Datapath with pipeline registers
slides.markdown:
Between each pair of stages sits a pipeline register (IF/ID, ID/EX, EX/MEM, MEM/WB) that latches everything the next stage needs.

![The 5-stage datapath with pipeline registers between IF, ID, EX, MEM, and WB](assets/five-stage-pipeline-registers.svg)

Without these, a changing signal could bleed into a later stage mid-cycle. They let each stage work on a *different* instruction than its neighbors, every cycle.

assets.alt: The 5-stage datapath with pipeline registers between IF, ID, EX, MEM, and WB

slides.subTitle: Data plus control signals
slides.markdown:
Each pipeline register carries two kinds of cargo: the **data** the instruction operates on (register values, an immediate, a computed address) and the **control signals** telling later stages what to do with it (is this a load? a branch? which register gets written?).

Control signals matter as much as data — a stage cycles downstream still needs to know "this is a store" even though decode happened earlier. Forgetting to carry a control signal forward is a classic from-scratch bug: the data survives, but the stage no longer knows what to *do* with it.

slides.subTitle: Balancing stage work
slides.markdown:
Five stages isn't arbitrary — it roughly balances the amount of work per stage so no single stage dominates the clock period. Fetch and decode are each a memory read; execute is one ALU operation; memory access is one more memory read/write; write-back is one register write.

If one stage did far more work than the others (say, combining decode and execute), that stage would set a much longer minimum clock period, and every *other* stage would sit idle waiting for it. Balanced stages mean the clock can run as fast as the slowest stage genuinely requires, not slower.

slides.subTitle: Four instructions, cycle by cycle
slides.markdown:
Four back-to-back independent instructions, one entering the pipeline each cycle:

```
Cycle:   1   2   3   4   5   6   7   8
I1:     IF  ID  EX  MEM WB
I2:         IF  ID  EX  MEM WB
I3:             IF  ID  EX  MEM WB
I4:                 IF  ID  EX  MEM WB
```

By cycle 4, all five stages are simultaneously occupied by four *different* instructions. I1 finishes at the end of cycle 5; from then on, one instruction finishes every single cycle — the pipeline is running at full throughput.

slides.subTitle: This pipeline vs modern depth
slides.markdown:
| | Classic 5-stage | Modern high-performance core |
|---|---|---|
| Stage count | 5 | 14-20+ |
| Per-stage work | Coarse (a whole ALU op) | Fine-grained, heavily split |
| Misprediction cost | Small (few cycles flushed) | Large (many cycles flushed) |
| Why deeper | — | Higher achievable clock speed |

The classic 5-stage design is the right teaching model because every stage maps cleanly to one conceptual step. Real high-performance CPUs go far deeper to push clock speed higher, at the cost of a much bigger penalty whenever a branch misprediction forces a flush — a trade-off you'll meet again in [Instruction-Level Parallelism](superscalar-execution).
